metadata.summary: This European interdisciplinary consensus guideline addresses invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in immunocompetent and immunosuppressed patients. Its first part updates definitions, epidemiology, diagnosis, prognostic risk assessment, staging and prevention, including chemoprevention. It is intended to support clinical care rather than replace national guidelines.

prophylaxis.recommendation: After transplantation, recommend an initial skin cancer risk assessment and education on photoprotection, self-skin examination and prompt recognition of suspicious lesions. recommended_regimens.name: Sun protection education
recommended_regimens.summary: Recommend education covering avoidance of sunbathing and artificial UVR tanning, protective clothing, and regular sunscreen use.

recommended_regimens.name: Behavioural counselling interventions
recommended_regimens.summary: Recommend counselling to improve sun-protective behaviour. The guideline notes limited evidence that behavioural interventions reduce sunburn or improve skin cancer outcomes.

recommended_regimens.name: Regular use of sunscreens
recommended_regimens.summary: Recommend regular sunscreen use. The guideline cites four prospective RCTs reporting a reduction in SCC incidence, while noting that two meta-analyses did not find a significant preventive effect for melanoma or nonmelanoma skin cancer.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Public health interventions to reduce UV exposure in the general population are also described in Box 7 with level of evidence 2. The guideline identifies shade and skin-covering clothing as the principal measures when exposure cannot be avoided.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Immunocompetent patients with a history of multiple cSCC
decision_rules: Nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily may be offered for chemoprevention, taking its favourable safety profile into account.
The reported benefit applied during active treatment; the guideline does not establish a persistent effect after treatment ends.

recommended_regimens.name: Nicotinamide
recommended_regimens.summary: May be offered at 500 mg twice daily to immunocompetent patients with multiple previous cSCCs. The cited randomized trial enrolled patients with a history of at least two nonmelanoma skin cancers.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the cited randomized trial, the rate of new cSCCs at 12 months was lower with nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily than with placebo, with a reduction by 30% compared to placebo, p = 0.05. A cited meta-analysis of 6–12 months of treatment reported a rate ratio of 0.48 (95% CI, 0.26–0.88) for new cSCC in high-risk patients and SOTRs compared with placebo-controls.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The cited randomized trial assessed treatment at 12 months; benefit was confined to the active treatment period.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline reports digestive adverse events with nicotinamide that resolved after dose reduction or withdrawal. Its recommendation for this population must not be extended to immunocompromised patients: a cited trial in OTRs found no significant between-group difference in new cSCCs and was underpowered.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients at risk of developing numerous or aggressive cSCCs
decision_rules: The guideline discusses topical 5% 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) as a chemopreventive treatment, but does not issue a formal recommendation or define eligibility criteria for its use.
The guideline reports that adding calcipotriol increases the benefit of 5-FU, without specifying a regimen.

alternative_regimens.name: 5% 5-fluorouracil (5-FU)
alternative_regimens.summary: A cited RCT found a reduction in cSCC requiring surgery during the first year after a topical course; the effect thereafter was not significant.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The guideline does not specify which patients should receive this course or present it as a formally recommended alternative.

alternative_regimens.name: calcipotriol to 5-FU
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline reports increased chemopreventive benefit when calcipotriol is added to 5-FU.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: No patient-selection criteria or treatment schedule are specified.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cited RCT used a 2–4 weeks course of 5-FU and reported a 75% reduction in cSCC requiring surgery, with protection apparent for one year and a non-significant effect thereafter. The guideline reports erythema in 92% and mild-to-moderate crusting in 61% of participants in the fluorouracil group. It reports no significant preventive effect for topical tretinoin but does not make a formal recommendation against it.

decision_rules: Recommend education on routine skin surveillance, sun protection, and sunscreen use.
Individualise photoprotection advice, including according to skin type.
For patients receiving azathioprine, use sunscreen providing substantial UVA protection throughout the year.

Following transplantation, recommend an initial skin cancer risk assessment and education on photoprotection, self-examination, and early recognition of suspicious lesions; determine later surveillance intervals from the initial risk assessment.

recommended_regimens.name: Sun protection measures and use of sunscreen
recommended_regimens.summary: Recommend education on photoprotection and sunscreen use alongside routine skin surveillance. The evidence level in Box 9 pertains to sunscreen in OTRs.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited non-randomised study reported a significant reduction in cSCC at 24 months with sunscreen.

response_assessment.method: Initial assessment of skin cancer risk based on age, gender, skin phototype and organ type
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the initial risk assessment to determine subsequent surveillance intervals.

supportive_care: Vitamin D monitoring is advisable because levels were lower in the sunscreen group of a cited study.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence that sunscreen prevents cSCC in immunosuppressed individuals is limited. The guideline states that behavioural interventions improve sun-protective behaviour in OTRs, but whether they prevent cSCC has not been confirmed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Solid organ transplant recipients with one or more cSCC
decision_rules: Conversion to mTOR inhibitors may be discussed with transplant physicians.
Modification of immunosuppression may be discussed with transplant physicians; consider allograft type, individual tumour risk and the rate of new tumours.
The guideline states that conversion from CNIs to mTOR inhibitors after a first cSCC reduces subsequent cSCC risk, whereas the reported reduction after more than one cSCC was non-significant.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral retinoids
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider oral retinoids for OTRs with one or more cSCC. The guideline cites consensus advice to begin acitretin at a low dose and increase it as tolerated to an effective maintenance dose.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline cites an estimated 54% overall reduction in cSCC in OTRs receiving retinoids.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Chemoprevention should be viewed as a long-term strategy. Cited consensus doses are 10 mg/day acitretin initially and up to 30 mg/ day acitretin for maintenance, as tolerated.

alternative_regimens.name: Conversion to mTOR inhibitors
alternative_regimens.summary: May be discussed with transplant physicians for OTRs with one or more cSCC. Cited RCTs found fewer subsequent cSCCs after conversion from CNIs following a first cSCC; after more than one cSCC, the reduction was non-significant.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider the adverse-effect profile and potential discontinuation; the guideline does not establish this conversion as preferred over oral retinoids.

alternative_regimens.name: Modification of immunosuppression
alternative_regimens.summary: May be discussed with transplant physicians as a secondary-prevention approach. The guideline notes limited evidence about when or how to modify treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider allograft type, tumour risk and rate of tumour accrual.

response_assessment.method: Liver function tests and lipid monitoring
response_assessment.interpretation: Laboratory monitoring is required because adverse effects may limit dosing.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline reports a common rebound increase in cSCCs 3–4 months after retinoid discontinuation. A cited meta-analysis found a 56% reduction in keratinocyte cancers with mTORi use but also reported increased overall mortality. An e-Delphi study recommended acitretin for OTRs with cSCC accrual > 10/year and as its first choice for high-risk cSCC; the guideline states that optimal sequencing remains to be established. Retinoids and capecitabine are not FDA/EMA approved for cSCC chemoprevention.

recommendations.statement: Classify common primary cSCC as either low-risk or high-risk. High-risk cSCC has no locoregional or distant metastasis (N0 and M0) but has features that increase the risk of local recurrence or metastasis.

recommendations.statement: Classify advanced cSCC as locally advanced (LacSCC), locoregional metastatic, or distant metastatic cSCC.
recommendations.source_heading: Box 1 Definitions and classifications of invasive cSCC

recommendations.statement: Define LacSCC as non-metastatic cSCC for which neither surgery nor radiotherapy offers a reasonable prospect of cure because of repeated recurrence, large size, bone erosion or invasion, infiltration beyond subcutaneous tissue into muscle or along nerves, or unacceptable complications, morbidity, or deformity from curative resection.

recommendations.statement: In the clinical assessment of primary cSCC, describe the lesion, document its symptoms and location, and measure its diameter.

recommendations.statement: Photographic documentation of primary cSCC is strongly recommended.

recommendations.statement: Dermatoscopy can assist with the preoperative differential diagnosis of cSCC.
recommendations.source_heading: Box 2 Clinical and non-invasive diagnosis of the primary cSCC

recommendations.statement: When available, confocal microscopy or OCT can assist with the preoperative differential diagnosis of cSCC.

recommendations.statement: Obtain histopathological confirmation when invasive SCC is suspected.
recommendations.source_heading: Box 3 Pathology report

recommendations.statement: The pathology report shall document specimen type, histological thickness or invasion depth, differentiation grade, whether perineural invasion is present, desmoplastic type, and margin status. It may additionally document histologic subtype, lymphovascular invasion, and the calibre of nerves affected by PNI if ≥0.1 mm.
recommendations.source_heading: Box 3 Pathology report

recommendations.statement: Consider the following proposed indicators of increased risk of local recurrence or nodal metastasis: tumour diameter > 20 mm; location on the lip, ear, or temple; thickness > 6 mm or invasion beyond subcutaneous fat; poor differentiation; desmoplasia; microscopic, symptomatic, or radiological PNI; bone erosion; immunosuppression; and positive surgical margins.
recommendations.context: Other histologic types, including acantholytic and adenosquamous types, have been linked to greater recurrence risk with less supporting evidence. Strength of consensus: 100%.
recommendations.rationale: These factors were proposed on the basis of evidence associating them with local recurrence or nodal metastasis.
recommendations.source_heading: Box 4 A proposed list of indicative prognostic high-risk factors for local recurrence or nodal metastasis of cSCC

recommendations.statement: For low-risk cSCC, use physical examination alone; imaging is unnecessary unless examination findings indicate it.
recommendations.source_heading: Box 5 Imaging for staging

recommendations.statement: In common primary cSCC with high-risk factors, assess for non-palpable regional lymph node involvement, preferably using US or CT scan.
recommendations.context: The guideline cannot specify which individual high-risk factors warrant imaging because their independent effects have not been reported consistently. Strength of consensus: 100%.
recommendations.source_heading: Box 5 Imaging for staging

recommendations.statement: If invasion of underlying bone or soft tissue is suspected, use CT or MRI to establish the extent of local infiltration.
recommendations.source_heading: Box 5 Imaging for staging

recommendations.statement: Perform imaging in LacSCC to exclude metastasis.
recommendations.source_heading: Box 5 Imaging for staging

recommendations.statement: For cSCC with nodal involvement, perform a complete skin examination and imaging to exclude distant metastatic disease.
recommendations.source_heading: Box 5 Imaging for staging

recommendations.statement: Do not use SLNB as standard care for cSCC at present.
recommendations.rationale: A prognostic advantage from detecting occult nodal metastasis with SLNB has not been established.

special_populations.considerations: A randomized trial in immunocompetent patients with a history of at least two nonmelanoma skin cancers found a lower rate of new cSCC during nicotinamide treatment at 12 months; the effect did not persist beyond active treatment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily may be offered to patients with a history of multiple cSCC in view of its favourable safety profile. In the cited trial, the reduction in new cSCC compared with placebo was 30% at 12 months (p = 0.05).

special_populations.considerations: This population bears a substantial and increasing cSCC burden. Evidence for choosing preventive treatments and deciding when to start them remains limited, especially outside organ transplant recipients. Strict photoprotection is usually advised, but direct evidence for cSCC prevention by sunscreen in immunosuppressed people is limited. Advice should be individualized, including by skin type. Other immunocompromised groups, particularly patients with CLL, may potentially benefit from risk-adapted surveillance.

Recipients have markedly increased cSCC rates. Following transplantation, baseline assessment of skin cancer risk and education on photoprotection, self-examination and early recognition of suspicious lesions are recommended; subsequent surveillance intervals depend on the initial risk assessment. Many post-transplant guidelines advise skin cancer surveillance at least annually, although evidence that this prevents cSCC is limited. In a sunscreen study, vitamin D levels were lower in the sunscreen group, making monitoring advisable. For patients receiving azathioprine, sunscreen providing substantial UVA protection should be used throughout the year. A trial of nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily for 12 months in 158 recipients found no significant difference in new cSCC versus placebo; poor recruitment left it underpowered.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Education about routine skin surveillance, sun protection and sunscreen use should be recommended. Oral retinoids should be considered after one or more cSCC; expert consensus describes starting acitretin at a low dose, such as 10 mg/day acitretin, and increasing it as tolerated to an effective maintenance dose, such as up to 30 mg/ day acitretin. This is a long-term approach requiring liver function and lipid monitoring. Conversion to mTOR inhibitors and modification of immunosuppression after one or more cSCC can be discussed with transplant physicians. Trials found fewer subsequent cSCC after conversion from CNIs to mTOR inhibitors following a first cSCC, but the reduction after more than one cSCC was non-significant; adverse effects and discontinuation are concerns. An e-Delphi study recommended acitretin for higher tumour accrual (> 10/year) and for high-risk cSCC, while optimal sequencing of preventive approaches remains unresolved.

conditions.name: invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
conditions.description: An invasive keratinocyte carcinoma arising from malignant epidermal keratinocytes that extend into the dermis. The guideline distinguishes common primary disease from locally advanced and metastatic disease; it excludes intra-epidermal lesions and mucosal SCC.
conditions.epidemiology: cSCC is the second most common skin cancer and accounts for 20% of keratinocyte carcinomas. Most primary tumours (80–90%) occur on the head and neck. Incidence rises with age, male sex and lower latitude; the standardized incidence ratio for male sex is 2.1 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.06–2.14). Incidence estimates are limited by inconsistent registration, particularly of multiple tumours. Increased rates occur in solid organ transplant recipients and people with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Compared with the general population, risk was 9–18-fold higher in Danish and US haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients. In a US cohort, among people who had already developed cSCC, those with HIV and CD4 count < 200 cells/mL had 2.2 times the subsequent cSCC risk of people without HIV.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Lesions commonly arise on sun-exposed skin, including the head, neck, forearms and backs of the hands. An early lesion may be a small skin-coloured papule or plaque with scale or hyperkeratosis; enlargement, crusting, ulceration and palpable induration may follow. Pigmentation can occur, particularly in non-white skin populations. Pain or tenderness can indicate perineural involvement. Appearance varies with differentiation, site, size, pigmentation and skin type.

staging.additional_rules: UICC 8th edition applies to skin sites other than eyelid, perianal, vulva and penis; AJCC 8th edition applies to head and neck cSCC. UICC T3 PNI concerns clinical or radiographic involvement of named nerves without foraminal or skull-base invasion or transgression. AJCC T3 also encompasses tumour in a nerve sheath deeper than the dermis or measuring 0.1 mm or larger. For both systems, deep invasion includes extension beyond subcutaneous fat or tumour thickness > 6 mm as specified in their respective definitions. If several cSCCs occur simultaneously, classify the tumour with the highest T category and indicate the number of separate tumours in parentheses, such as T2(5). Neither BWH nor Breuninger/Tübingen provides N or M categories. The listed cSCC staging systems do not incorporate satellite or in-transit metastases.

conditions.name: common primary cSCC
conditions.description: The usually readily treatable, non-metastatic primary form of cSCC. It is classified as low-risk or high-risk according to features associated with recurrence and metastasis.
conditions.epidemiology: Most treated primary cSCCs have a favourable prognosis, with 5-year cure rates greater than 90%. A single-centre study of more than 900 patients followed for approximately 10 years reported recurrence in 4.6%, nodal disease in 3.7% and disease-specific death in 2.1%. A prospective study of 615 surgically resected cases reported 3% local recurrence and 4% metastasis after a median follow up of 43 months. A UK cohort reported 2.7% recurrence and 1.2% metastasis; 85% of its metastases originated from head and neck cSCC.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Clinical appearance varies from a small scaly or hyperkeratotic papule or plaque to an enlarging, indurated, crusted or ulcerated tumour. Well-differentiated lesions tend to be hyperkeratotic or verrucous; poorly differentiated lesions can appear red, non-keratotic, ulcerated or bleeding.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) accounts for 20% of cutaneous malignancies in white populations. Most treated cases have a favourable prognosis, with 5-year cure rates greater than 90%, but the high incidence produces a substantial total number of deaths. Experts from EADO, EDF, ESTRO, UEMS, EADV and EORTC updated guidance using published evidence and consensus. Part 1 covers classification, epidemiology, diagnosis, prognostic risk, staging and prevention in immunocompetent and immunosuppressed patients.

document_sections.heading: 1. Information about the guidelines
document_sections.content: This update addresses invasive cSCC. Its first part covers definitions, epidemiology, etiopathogenesis, diagnosis, risk classification, staging and prevention; the accompanying part 2 addresses treatment, supportive care, patient education and follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 1.1. Societies in charge
document_sections.content: EDF initiated the guidelines following its January 2017 meeting. EADO coordinated contributions with ESTRO, UEMS and EADV, while EORTC participated to support an interdisciplinary approach. Alexander J. Stratigos, Claus Garbe and Jean-Jacques Grob coordinated the work. Thirty-five experts representing medical societies in 16 countries contributed.

document_sections.heading: 1.3. Disclaimer
document_sections.content: Diagnostic and therapeutic statements reflect knowledge available when the guidelines were prepared and may become outdated. Users remain responsible for clinical decisions, medications and doses; they are advised to check manufacturers’ information and seek specialist advice when uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 1.4. Scope
document_sections.content: The guidance supports clinicians diagnosing, monitoring and treating invasive cSCC. Developments in systemic therapy and evidence concerning prognostic factors, imaging and adjuvant radiotherapy prompted revised definitions, risk categories and multidisciplinary management strategies.

document_sections.heading: 1.5. Target population
document_sections.content: The two guideline parts address diagnosis, follow-up and treatment of people with invasive cSCC. They are intended for treating physicians and nursing staff, with recommendations presented so patients can also understand them.

document_sections.heading: 1.6. Objectives and formulation of questions
document_sections.content: The subject is invasive cSCC, not early intra-epidermal SCC-like actinic keratoses (AK), Bowen’s disease or mucosal SCCs, including genital and labialbuccal-nasal lesions sometimes grouped with head and neck tumours. The guidance emphasizes definitions, diagnosis, risk classification, staging and treatment, and also addresses education and prevention.

document_sections.heading: 1.7. Audience and period of validity
document_sections.content: The guidance assists healthcare providers but does not supersede accepted national guidelines or replace individualized decisions. Later studies may change its conclusions. Updates are anticipated approximately every 2 years, with an expiration date of December 2025, or sooner if scientific developments warrant.

document_sections.heading: 1.8. Methods
document_sections.content: A unified guideline was issued in two linked parts and updates the 2020 European consensus guidance. Other contemporary guidance informed it. Authors searched English-language Medline publications initially through November 1, 2022, checked references of selected papers, and updated the search on 10th March 2023. Development followed AGREE II standards. Recommendations draw on the best available evidence and good clinical practice points (GPP). Evidence follows the Oxford classification: level 1 represents the strongest evidence, level 2 randomized or well-designed cohort or cross-sectional studies, level 3 adequately designed non-randomized studies, and levels 4 and 5 weaker evidence involving fewer patients or poorer quality. Study quality, imprecision, indirectness, inconsistency or a very small absolute effect can lower a level; a large or very large effect can raise it. Recommendation grades are A for a strong recommendation, B for a recommendation, C for a weak recommendation, X for an intervention that should not be recommended, and 0 when evidence is unavailable or insufficient to recommend for or against. Expert consensus supplies GPP where adequate evidence is lacking. Reviewers from participating societies who were not authors also assessed the manuscripts. Table 1 presents the Oxford evidence levels by clinical question.

document_sections.heading: 1.9. Consensus building process
document_sections.content: Experts experienced in national guidance drafted the initial text; EORTC then selected contributors from additional specialties. At a Rome meeting on 25th November 2022, Twentyfour experts approved the text and reached at least 80% agreement on recommendations in structured boxes and the figure. Voting allowed agreement, disagreement, abstention and comments. A prevention box for solid organ transplant recipients was added afterward. The 10th March 2023 literature update did not change the recommendation boxes, although references and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 were updated. Co-authors finalized the text by email in the first semester 2023. Compared with 2020, Boxes 4 and 7 were retained, Boxes 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 were revised, and Boxes 8 and 9 were added.

document_sections.heading: 2. Definitions of cSCC
document_sections.content: cSCC arises from malignant epidermal keratinocyte proliferation and, like basal cell carcinoma, is a keratinocyte carcinoma. It has in situ and invasive forms; invasive disease probably often follows prolonged intraepidermal dysplasia. This guidance concerns invasive disease. Common primary cSCC is non-metastatic and usually treatable; recurrence risk separates it into low-risk and high-risk categories. High-risk cSCC has features associated with greater recurrence or metastatic risk but no locoregional or distant metastasis, is staged N0 and M0, and remains amenable to curative surgery or radiotherapy (RT). Advanced disease comprises locally advanced (lacSCC) and metastatic (mcSCC) disease. LacSCC is non-metastatic but cannot reasonably be cured with surgery or radiotherapy because of factors such as repeated recurrence, size, bone involvement, extension beyond subcutaneous tissue into muscle or along nerves, or unacceptable consequences of curative resection; it corresponds to unresectable T3/T4 in the 8th edition AJCC or UICC classification. McSCC includes in-transit, regional nodal and distant metastases requiring systemic treatment. Regional nodal disease corresponds to stage III or IV and distant disease to stage IV; in-transit metastases are not represented in the 8th edition AJCC/UICC systems.

document_sections.heading: Box 1 Definitions and classifications of invasive cSCC.
document_sections.content: Grade of recommendation: A; Level of evidence: 1; Strength of consensus: 100%. Common primary cSCC shall be categorized as low-risk or high-risk. High-risk disease has recurrence- or metastasis-associated features without in-transit, regional nodal or distant metastasis and is N0 and M0. Advanced cSCC shall be categorized as locally advanced, locoregional metastatic or distant metastatic. LacSCC shall denote non-metastatic disease for which neither surgery nor radiotherapy offers a reasonable prospect of cure because of repeated recurrence, size, bone erosion or invasion, deep extension into muscle or along nerves, or unacceptable morbidity, complications or deformity from curative surgery.

document_sections.heading: 3. Epidemiology
document_sections.content: cSCC is the second most common skin cancer and accounts for 20% of keratinocyte carcinomas; basal cell carcinoma-to-cSCC ratios range from 2 to 4:1. Most primary lesions, 80–90%, occur on the head and neck. Incidence estimates are limited partly because some datasets include AK or in situ disease, but available data indicate rising rates in most white populations, with further increases predicted. Table 2 compares international age-standardized incidence. Incidence rises with age, male sex (standardized incidence ratio, 2.1; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.06–2.14) and lower latitude; multiple tumours correlate strongly with age. In the United Kingdom during 2013–2015, 62.7% of cases occurred in men, whose median age was 80 years, and the mean annual percentage increase was 5%. Norwegian age-adjusted incidence rose nine-fold in females and six-fold in males from 1963 to 2011, particularly at ages 70–79 years. Swedish registry data linked higher incidence at the same latitude to sunnier coastal residence. The Rochester Epidemiology Project reported a 263% incidence increase between 1976 and 1984 and 2000–2010, disproportionately affecting women and people under 40 years. Inconsistent registration, sometimes recording only a first tumour, substantially understates the public-health burden. Higher rates occur after solid organ transplantation and with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Danish and US haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients had 9–18-fold greater risk than the general population. In a US cohort, patients with HIV and CD4 count < 200 cells/mL had a 2.2 times higher risk of another cSCC after their first than uninfected people.

document_sections.heading: 3.1. Prognosis
document_sections.content: Properly and promptly treated common primary cSCC usually behaves indolently; overall 5-year cure rates exceed 90%. A single-centre study of more than 900 patients followed for approximately 10 years reported recurrence of 4.6%, nodal disease of 3.7% and disease-specific death of 2.1%. A prospective study of 615 surgically treated patients reported 3% local recurrence and 4% metastasis after median follow-up of 43 months. A large UK cohort reported 2.7% recurrence and 1.2% metastasis, with 85% of metastases originating from head and neck lesions. UK National Cancer Registration and Analysis Service data from 2013–15 estimated cumulative locoregional or distant metastasis incidence at 2.1% after median follow-up of 15.2 months: 1.1% in women and 2.4% in men. Of mcSCC cases, 85.2% were identified within 2 years of primary cSCC; head and neck or parotid lymph nodes were the metastatic site in 73.6%. Risk increased with age, male sex, immunosuppression, greater deprivation, and ear or lip location. Studies generally report worse outcomes under immunosuppression: more locoregional recurrence, at least doubled metastatic risk and significantly worse advanced-disease outcomes. The US transplant population had reported mortality of 494 per 100,000. CLL has also been linked to greater recurrence, nodal spread and death, while survival after nodal disease is significantly lower in immunosuppressed people. Epidermolysis bullosa can cause early, aggressive and multiple tumours at chronically blistered or scarred sites; among 31 people with severe recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa in a UK study spanning 1991–2019, 52% developed metastatic disease, and cSCC was the leading cause of death. Norwegian registry data from 2000 to 2011 reported 5-year relative survival for localized cSCC of 88% in women and 82% in men, versus 64% in women and 51% in men with advanced disease. A prospective series of 2149 cSCC in 1434 patients reported 2.8% disease-specific death after median follow-up of 36.5 months. Local complications and destruction of underlying tissue in lacSCC, as well as metastases, can cause disease-specific death.

document_sections.heading: 4. Aetiology and pathogenesis
document_sections.content: Ultraviolet radiation (UVR), from sunlight or tanning beds, is the predominant causal exposure. Other implicated factors include immunosuppression, BRAF inhibitor (BRAFi) monotherapy, β-HPV subtypes and smoking. Although cSCC frequently develops amid AK and chronic photodamage, clinically apparent AK progresses at less than 1/1000 per year during a 5-year follow up. In metastatic melanoma, vemurafenib, dabrafenib or encorafenib alone carries greater cSCC risk than combined BRAF/MEK inhibitors. A proposed explanation is paradoxical activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway and keratinocyte proliferation in wild-type BRAF cells, particularly with oncogenic RAS mutations. cSCC has been reported during vismodegib treatment for advanced basal cell carcinoma, but a treatment relationship is uncertain. Photosensitizing antihypertensives have been associated with cSCC risk; hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) has a dose-dependent association. In 2018, EMA recommended product-information warnings about keratinocyte carcinoma and possible reconsideration of HCTZ in patients with prior disease. Bendroflumethiazide was not associated with any skin cancer type and was suggested as a potentially safer alternative TZ for patients at increased risk.

document_sections.heading: 4.1. Molecular pathogenesis
document_sections.content: cSCC has a high mutation burden, with a median of 45.2 mutations per megabase [Mb] of genomic DNA. Most tumours show a UV-associated C > T or CC > TT signature. Sun-exposed normal skin and AK have lower mutation rates, although many contain NOTCH1 and TP53 driver mutations; whether they are clonally related true precursors remains uncertain. Reported alterations include TP53, CDKN2A, NOTCH1, NOTCH2, KMT2C, KMT2D, TET2, Hippo-pathway and SWI/SNF-complex genes, and inactivating changes in transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) receptors. Potentially targetable PIK3CA, FGFR3, BRAF and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) alterations are uncommon. Mutation signatures have been linked to azathioprine exposure and recessive epidermolysis bullosa, and possibly to tumours arising in burn scars or chronic ulcers. An APOBEC-associated profile was reported in 100% of cSCC tumors from patients with recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa. Genome-wide studies associate cSCC risk with MC1R, ASIP, TYR, SLC45A2, OCA2, IRF4, BNC2, CADM1, AHR, SEC16A, TYRP1, TRSP1, HLA variants, BACH2, SETDB1, ECM1 and CERS2. Primary tumours that did not progress contained more CD8+ and CD4+ T-cells than high-risk tumours in a cited study. PD-L1 was detected in around 26% of primary lesions and up to 50% of metastases. Predisposing hereditary conditions include xeroderma pigmentosum, epidermolysis bullosa, congenital epidermodysplasia verruciformis, oculocutaneous albinism, Fanconi anaemia and Lynch syndrome/Muir Torre syndrome.

document_sections.heading: 5. Diagnostic approach in primary cSCC
document_sections.content: Evaluation combines clinical assessment and documentation with histological confirmation. Non-invasive methods can assist differential diagnosis, but the evidence does not support routine diagnostic use of every available imaging technique.

document_sections.heading: 5.1. Clinical diagnosis
document_sections.content: Appearance varies with size, differentiation, pigmentation, location and skin type; sun-exposed head, neck, forearms and dorsal hands are common sites. Multiple AK predict subsequent cSCC in previously unaffected people. Early minimally invasive disease often appears as a small flesh-coloured, scaly or hyperkeratotic papule or plaque resembling AK or Bowen’s disease. Lesions may enlarge, ulcerate, crust and become indurated. Pigmentation may be more apparent in non-white skin. Well-differentiated tumours are often hyperkeratotic, verrucous or crateriform; poorly differentiated lesions may be red, non-keratinizing, ulcerated or bleeding and resemble other tumours. Tenderness or spontaneous pain may indicate perineural involvement. Keratoacanthoma is treated as a well-differentiated cSCC subtype with distinctive histology; it generally does not arise from AK, grows over a few weeks, can occasionally regress, and usually forms a symmetric, keratin-capped dome-shaped nodule on sun-exposed skin. LacSCC may follow aggressive biology, repeated relapse after inadequate initial treatment or neglect, producing large indurated, infiltrative lesions that can invade structures such as the orbit or sinuses and cause pain. Examination alone cannot reliably determine full extent or depth. McSCC may manifest through in-transit, nodal or distant deposits. Draining-basin examination and, when metastasis must be excluded in high-risk disease, imaging should be considered. Differential diagnoses include inflamed seborrheic keratosis, high-grade AK, keratotic basal cell carcinoma, amelanotic melanoma, atypical fibroxanthoma, Merkel cell carcinoma and adnexal tumours. Before biopsy or surgery, the record should contain maximum clinical diameter, location and symptoms; clinical photography and, where possible, dermatoscopic images are recommended. Clinical diameter informs risk and stage, whereas specimen shrinkage can reduce the measured histological size.

document_sections.heading: 5.2. Dermatoscopy and other non-invasive techniques
document_sections.content: Dermatoscopy is part of skin-tumour assessment. Well-differentiated cSCC often shows keratin masses, white structureless areas, perifollicular white circles or white halos around hairpin or coiled vessels. Keratin is frequent but nonspecific. White structureless areas favour cSCC over AK, and perifollicular white circles help distinguish it from several other nodular tumours. Perivascular halos also occur in benign keratinizing lesions, but their distribution tends to be irregular in cSCC rather than homogeneous. Keratoacanthoma commonly has central keratin surrounded by radially arranged hairpin or coiled vessels with white halos. Poorly differentiated cSCC is more often red, with diverse vessel shapes, frequent haemorrhage and no keratinization signs. Moderately differentiated lesions combine white and vascular findings. Evidence from limited case series is insufficient for routine diagnostic use of Reflectance Confocal Microscopy (RCM), Line field confocal OCT (LC-OCT) or Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT). RCM findings can correspond to parakeratosis, atypical keratinocytes and vascular changes, but shallow laser penetration can prevent full-thickness assessment; distinguishing cSCC from BCC is a possible use. LC-OCT and OCT offer deeper vertical views that may help distinguish in situ from early invasive disease. Table 3 lists the WHO classification of skin SCC and its codes.

document_sections.heading: Box 2 Clinical and non-invasive diagnosis of the primary cSCC.
document_sections.content: Consensus-based GPP; Strength of consensus: 100%. Clinical assessment should describe the lesion, symptoms, site and diameter. Photographic documentation is strongly recommended. Preoperative differential diagnosis can be assisted by dermatoscopy and, if available, confocal microscopy or OCT.

document_sections.heading: 5.3. Histopathological diagnosis
document_sections.content: Histology is the diagnostic reference standard; clinically suspected cSCC should undergo biopsy or excision with histological confirmation. A lower biopsy threshold has been proposed for solid organ transplant recipients. Initial sampling may be incisional, by incision or punch, or excisional, according to lesion size and planned treatment. The longest clinical diameter, including surrounding erythema, should be documented before surgery because it contributes to prognostic staging. Invasive cSCC contains atypical epithelial formations extending into dermis and may show cornification and horny pearls. Table 3 gives the WHO classification, 4th edition, 2018. Desmoplastic cSCC is not yet included there; its infiltrative, perineural or perivascular growth makes it a high-risk histological subtype in NCCN guidance. Requests for biopsy and excision should state patient demographics, site and clinical diameter. The final excision report should document tumour thickness, invasion depth, perineural invasion (PNI) status, differentiation, desmoplastic type and margins; subtype, lymphovascular invasion and the calibre of involved nerves if ≥0.1 mm are additional useful findings. Under AJCC 8th edition, vertical thickness runs from the granular layer of adjacent normal epidermis to the tumour base, in mm. Invasion depth should identify extension into subcutaneous fat (Clark level V) or deeper. PNI reporting needs standardization. Desmoplastic, metaplastic (spindle cell), acantholytic (adenoid) and adenosquamous subtypes have been associated with increased recurrence or metastatic risk and are NCCN high-risk criteria. The authors propose diagnosing desmoplasia when at least one third of the specimen contains infiltrating atypical squamous nests, often single-cell strands, within a conspicuous sclerotic stromal response. Well-differentiated tumours generally have lower metastatic potential than poorly differentiated tumours. Table 4 provides the histopathology-report checklist.

document_sections.heading: Box 3 Pathology report.
document_sections.content: Consensus-based GPP; Strength of consensus: 100%. Suspected invasive SCC shall receive histopathological diagnosis. Reports shall include specimen type, histological thickness or invasion depth, differentiation grade, PNI status, desmoplastic type and margin status. They may additionally report subtype, lymphovascular invasion and involved-nerve calibre when PNI affects nerves ≥0.1 mm.

document_sections.heading: 6. Prognostic factors for high-risk cSCC
document_sections.content: High-risk cSCC has recurrence- or metastasis-associated features without locoregional or distant spread and is staged N0 and M0. Identifying such factors among common primary tumours affects decisions about more extensive surgery and closer follow-up. Reported factors include clinical diameter, thickness, invasion level, desmoplasia, poor differentiation, PNI, site and immunosuppression. Evidence and guideline criteria vary, although major guidelines share several highest-risk features; Table 5 compares them. Retrospective studies often have few patients, heterogeneous populations or different endpoints. The proposed European list distinguishes tumour-related factors from patient- and treatment-related factors and includes clinical, histological and radiological findings plus immunosuppression. In a prospective study, Haug et al. observed PNI only in desmoplastic cSCC and found thickness ≥6 mm, size ≥20 mm, immunosuppression, PNI and desmoplasia independently associated with recurrence or metastasis. Meta-analyses associated immunosuppression independently with disease-specific death; a prospective study of 1400 patients also found this association, whereas a retrospective study did not, although its immunosuppressed groups had only 25 deaths. Positive margins indicate residual tumour; incomplete initial removal increases recurrence, mainly locally. Among Mohs-treated patients in a retrospective study, only poor differentiation and extension beyond subcutaneous fat correlated with worse outcomes. Recurrence itself was not added as a high-risk factor for another recurrence because an underlying factor may account for the initial event. Updated analyses indicate that individual factors affect local recurrence, nodal metastasis and disease-specific death differently. In BWH staging, combining two or more of poor differentiation, PNI, clinical diameter and invasion beyond subcutaneous tissue significantly increases adverse-outcome risk. Because precise individual-factor risks remain uncertain, assessment should account for variation in tumour and patient characteristics. A developed and validated 40-gene expression profile (GEP) test predicted metastasis risk in localized high-risk disease; combining 40-GEP with clinicopathological factors improved metastatic-risk classification.

document_sections.heading: Box 4 A proposed list of indicative prognostic high-risk factors for local recurrence or nodal metastasis of cSCC.
document_sections.content: Grade of recommendation: B; Level of evidence: 2; Strength of consensus: 100%. Indicative factors are diameter > 20 mm; lip, ear or temple location; thickness > 6 mm or invasion past subcutaneous fat; poor differentiation; desmoplasia; microscopic, symptomatic or radiological PNI; bone erosion; immunosuppression; and positive surgical margins. Acantholytic and adenosquamous histology have also been linked to recurrence, but supporting evidence is weaker. One cited study defined immunosuppression by organ transplantation, HIV, chronic lymphatic leukaemia or another haematological malignancy; the cited meta-analyses did not define it specifically. Zakhem et al. reported higher local-recurrence risk after transplantation and with HIV, and higher nodal-metastasis risk after transplantation.

document_sections.heading: 7. Staging systems for cSCC
document_sections.content: Four general staging systems are described: UICC 8th edition, AJCC 8th edition, BWH and Breuninger/Tübingen. N1S3 and ITEM additionally address head and neck nodal disease; Tables 6–8 compare classifications. UICC and AJCC T categories chiefly use size, with depth and PNI as additional factors. The text notes different handling of tumours measuring 2 cm and different PNI definitions: UICC specifies clinical or radiographic named-nerve involvement without foramen or skull-base extension, whereas AJCC also includes a nerve deeper than dermis or ≥0.1 mm in calibre. BWH counts diameter ≥2 cm, poor differentiation, PNI in nerve(s) ≥0.1 mm and invasion beyond subcutaneous fat; T category rises with the number of factors. Neither BWH nor Breuninger supplies N or M categories. In a study of 680 head and neck cases, AJCC8 T3/T4 and BWH T2b/T3 identified 121 (18%) versus 63 (9%) cases, 17 (71%) versus 16 (70%) metastases, and 11 (85%) versus 12 (92%) deaths. AJCC8 T2 and T3 together comprised 23% of cases and had statistically indistinguishable outcomes. The authors reported BWH specificity of 93% and positive predictive value of 30% for metastasis or death, without differences in local recurrence or overall survival. A proposed Salamanca refinement of AJCC8 T3 was not validated as an improvement in a study of 1774 cSCC. In a case comparison involving 887 metastatic and 887 non-metastatic tumours, BWH had the highest specificity (92.8%, 95% CI 90.8–94.3%) and c-index (0.84, 95% CI 0.82–0.86), but every system had low positive predictive value. That study assumed reported PNI met the ≥0.1 mm criterion, potentially misclassifying tumours with nerve calibre < 0.1 mm. Another comparison favoured BWH and Breuninger for predicting metastasis: Breuninger high co-risk factors gave OR: 3.27; 95% CI:1.54–6.96, while BWH gave ORs of 6.58 (95% CI: 2.90–14.90) for T2a and 35.34 (95% CI: 9.76–128.06) for T2b. Its authors considered existing systems unsatisfactory for identifying high-risk patients in unselected populations. AJCC8 pathological nodal classification also applies to mucosal head and neck cancer; a cited cSCC comparison found extranodal extension performed poorly as a predictor because it was common in the studied population. N1S3 uses nodal size ≤3 versus > 3 cm and single versus multiple nodes. ITEM scores immunosuppression, treatment, extranodal spread and margin status. N1S3 performed best in a comparison, although prediction remained relatively poor: disease-specific survival C-index 0.62 and proportion of variation explained 10.9%; overall survival C-index 0.59 and proportion of variation explained 4.5%. In a study of 1128 patients with head and neck nodal metastasis, groups comprised 1–2 nodes (N = 816), 3–4 nodes (N = 162) and ≥5 nodes (N = 150). Against the reference group, disease-specific mortality increased for 3–4 nodes (Hazard ratio [HR], 1.58; 95% CI: 1.03–2.42; p = 0.036) and ≥five nodes (HR, 2.91; 95% CI: 1.99–4.25; p < 0.001), with similar all-cause findings; the authors judged node count more informative than TNM stage. cSCC staging systems omit satellitosis or in-transit metastasis (S-ITM). In a cohort of 518 patients, including 72 node-negative patients with S-ITM, 2-year cumulative recurrence incidence was 18.8% (95% CI, 18.7–18.9%) for T3N0, 28.6% (95% CI, 27.5–29.8%) for T4N0, 53.2% (95% CI, 52.4–54.0%) for N1 to 3%, and 56.6% (95% CI, 55.9–57.3%) for S-ITM. Disease-specific survival with S-ITM resembled that of node-positive patients; the study authors proposed including these deposits in staging.

document_sections.heading: 8. Staging work-up
document_sections.content: Fig. 1 presents the diagnostic and staging algorithm, with Strength of consensus: 100%. Recurrent cSCC is staged using the same approach as primary disease.

document_sections.heading: 8.1. Physical examination
document_sections.content: After cSCC diagnosis, examination should assess the primary site, the entire skin for other cancers, AK, photodamage, inflammatory disease and features of predisposition, and the primary-site surface for in-transit metastases. Although nodal involvement risk is relatively low, up to 5%, every patient should have careful examination and palpation of regional nodal basins. This usually suffices for low-risk cSCC. A clinically or radiologically detected regional node warrants recommended fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC); ultrasound-guided core biopsy is an alternative.

document_sections.heading: 8.2. Nodal imaging
document_sections.content: Evidence establishing when to stage with imaging is limited. For common primary disease without palpable nodes, imaging is recommended only when EADO high-risk factors are present. US, CT and PET-CT are more sensitive than clinical examination, but direct cSCC evidence for nodal US is limited. In a study of 44 patients with vulvar cSCC and suspected inguinal metastasis, US had higher sensitivity and negative predictive value than CT, but lower specificity and positive predictive value. A meta-analysis of 17 studies in head and neck SCC, not specifically cSCC, found the highest diagnostic odds ratios with US-guided FNAC; US significantly outperformed MRI, with mean US sensitivity of 87% and US-guided FNAC specificity of 98%. Only two studies examined clinically N0 necks. Baseline or surveillance imaging in a retrospective series of 87 high-risk patients detected disease in 26 (30%), including 18 subclinical cases. In another retrospective series of 246 high-risk head and neck cSCC cases, baseline nodal US had sensitivity 91% and specificity 78%, compared with 50% and 96% for examination alone. Its authors cautioned that greater sensitivity must be weighed against false positives investigated by FNAC. Experienced-operator US may offer a minimally invasive, cost-effective way to assess superficial cSCC nodal metastases.

document_sections.heading: 8.3. Imaging for lacSCC and distant metastasis
document_sections.content: Advanced cSCC staging requires multidisciplinary tumour-board input, including a radiologist, to select imaging. Large tumours or suspected orbital, perineural, bone or other deep involvement may require CT or MRI to delineate local and metastatic extent. MRI is indicated for subtle intracranial involvement, perineural spread and surrounding soft-tissue invasion. CT and PET-CT are suitable for detecting distant-organ metastases. Whether imaging improves treatment choice and disease course remains important to establish. In a retrospective study of 45 patients with BWH T2b or T3 disease, imaging was mainly CT (79%), PET/CT or MRI, with no US use; management changed for 16 (33%).

document_sections.heading: Box 5 Imaging for staging.
document_sections.content: Evidence-based GPP; Level of evidence: 3; Strength of consensus: 100%. Low-risk cSCC should be assessed by physical examination without imaging unless examination indicates it. Common primary cSCC with high-risk features should be assessed for non-palpable nodal disease, preferably with US or CT. Suspected bone or soft-tissue extension calls for CT or MRI to define infiltration. LacSCC should be imaged to exclude metastasis. Nodal disease calls for complete skin examination and imaging to exclude distant spread. Evidence does not permit precise specification of which individual high-risk factors trigger nodal imaging; higher-risk categories include, but are not limited to, AJCC8 T3/T4 and BWH T2b/T3.

document_sections.heading: 8.4. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB)
document_sections.content: SLNB seeks occult nodal disease, but an improvement in prognosis from its detection has not been established. A systematic review of 23 studies reported positive SLNB in 8% and found no adjusted evidence on predictors or prognostic utility. Another review found positivity of 13.9% (32 of 231 patients) and a false-negative rate of 4.6%; available studies were small and heterogeneous. A meta-analysis of 19 studies involving 130 patients with non-anogenital cSCC reported sentinel-node microscopic involvement in 12.3%, all with tumours larger than 2 cm. Positivity varied from 0% in AJCC T1 to 60% in AJCC T4, and was 7.1% (6/85) for BWH T2a, 29.4% (5/17) for BWH T2b and 50% (3/6) for BWH T3. A retrospective comparison of 720 patients whose tumours were at least 6 mm thick included 150 receiving SLNB and 570 observed. Sentinel nodes were positive in 3.96% of biopsied patients. After median follow-up of 3 years, nodal metastasis did not differ significantly between groups (11.9% and 11.4%, respectively), nor did tumour-specific death (7.14% versus 4.74%). A cost-effectiveness model favoured omitting SLNB at every stage, attributing this to low nodal-metastasis and disease-specific mortality rates. A review of 705 patients from 20 studies found a pooled identification rate of 98.8%, positivity of 5.6% and cumulative regional recurrence of 2.9% after negative SLNB; its authors questioned clinical utility despite procedural feasibility. Because prognostic benefit is unproven and beneficiaries are not defined, SLNB cannot currently be recommended as standard care.

document_sections.heading: Box 6 Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB).
document_sections.content: Grade of recommendation: X; Level of evidence: 3; Strength of consensus: 100%. SLNB is not currently recommended as standard management for cSCC. The cited evidence has not established a prognostic advantage from identifying occult nodal metastases.

document_sections.heading: 9. Primary and secondary prevention
document_sections.content: Chronic or intermittent ambient UV exposure, through work or recreation during childhood or adulthood, increases cSCC risk. Population-level UV-reduction measures can cost-effectively reduce skin-cancer incidence and healthcare costs. Behavioural interventions improve sun-protective practices, but evidence that they prevent sunburn or improve cancer outcomes is limited. Combined approaches, including media campaigns, shade provision, early-childhood family counselling and digital interventions, are considered most effective for changing exposure behaviour. Advice includes avoiding sun between 10 am and 4 pm, covering skin, using broad-spectrum sunscreen and avoiding tanning beds; favourable attitudes toward tanning impede implementation. Four randomized trials and several non-randomized prospective experimental studies reported fewer AK and cSCC with regular sunscreen use in general and transplant populations. Two meta-analyses found no significant preventive effectiveness against melanoma or nonmelanoma skin cancer, but included retrospective studies and studies limited to UVB filters. Shade and protective clothing remain the primary measures; regular sunscreen is recommended as a third measure if exposure cannot be avoided. Everyone with prior cSCC should receive clear strict-photoprotection advice. Outdoor workers may need occupational measures; risk-adapted screening has been developed for transplant recipients in Australia and the UK. Table-independent recommendations appear in Box 7.

document_sections.heading: Box 7 Prevention.
document_sections.content: Evidence-based GPP; Strength of consensus: 100%. Education recommending avoidance of sunbathing and artificial UVR tanning, protective clothing and regular sunscreen shall be provided. Behavioural counselling shall be recommended (Level of evidence 1), as shall regular sunscreen use (Level of evidence 1). The box also identifies population-wide interventions to reduce UV exposure (Level of evidence 2).

document_sections.heading: 10. Chemoprevention
document_sections.content: Chemoprevention aims to reduce new cSCC, particularly in people prone to numerous or aggressive tumours. Studied systemic agents include retinoids, nicotinamide and NSAIDS. Acitretin and isotretinoin reduced new tumours during treatment in high-risk patients but are not routinely recommended because of teratogenicity and poorly tolerated dose-related adverse effects. Nicotinamide may support repair of UV-damaged DNA and counter UV-associated immune inhibition. A meta-analysis found fewer new cSCC during 6–12 months of nicotinamide in high-risk patients and SOTRs than with placebo (rate ratio 0.48 (95% CI, 0.26–0.88). In one trial of 386 immunocompetent people with at least two previous nonmelanoma skin cancers, nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily reduced new cSCC by 30% compared with placebo at 12 months (p = 0.05); benefit was confined to active treatment. It was generally tolerated, although increased digestive adverse events resolved after dose reduction or withdrawal. A 2015 meta-analysis associated NSAIDS with lower cSCC risk but had significant heterogeneity. A UK case-control study found a small reduction among regular NSAIDS users (OR: 0.89, 95% CI: 0.82–0.97), whereas an Australian cohort found inconsistent associations and no convincing preventive evidence. Evidence for antioxidants, phytochemicals and selenium is inconclusive. Vitamin D3 plus calcium did not significantly reduce new self-reported nonmelanoma skin cancers in a trial of 36,282 postmenopausal women; vitamin D alone did not significantly reduce cSCC in a trial of 2259 participants. In one trial, topical 5% 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) reduced cSCC requiring surgery by 75%; a 2–4 weeks course appeared protective for one year but not significantly thereafter. In its treatment group, 92% reported erythema and 61% mild-to-moderate crusting. Adding calcipotriol increased the reported benefit. Topical tretinoin did not significantly prevent cSCC.

document_sections.heading: Box 8 Nicotinamide for chemoprevention in immunocompetent patients with a history of multiple cSCC.
document_sections.content: Grade of recommendation C; Level of evidence 3; Strength of consensus: 100%. Nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily may be offered to immunocompetent people with multiple previous cSCC, taking its favourable safety profile into account. A cited randomized trial reported 30% fewer new cSCC at 12 months (p = 0.05).

document_sections.heading: 11. Prevention in immunocompromised patients
document_sections.content: cSCC places a substantial and growing burden on immunocompromised people. Education, surveillance adjusted to risk, prevention and rapid diagnostic and treatment access may reduce that burden. Most prevention evidence and consensus address organ transplant recipients (OTRs); evidence remains limited for choosing and sequencing interventions or defining when to start them.

document_sections.heading: 11.1. Primary prevention in immunocompromised patients
document_sections.content: Strict protection through sunscreen, clothing and behaviour is usually recommended, drawing partly on immunocompetent-population evidence. Direct evidence in immunosuppressed people is limited to a non-randomized open-label sunscreen trial reporting significantly fewer cSCC at 24 months. Vitamin D levels were lower with sunscreen, so monitoring is advisable. Because azathioprine is associated with UVA photosensitivity, sunscreen with substantial UVA protection should be used throughout the year. Specialist-setting, individualized advice is better recalled and followed, and should reflect skin type. Written materials, text messages, apps and videos improve OTRs’ protective behaviour, knowledge, attitudes and biological measures of UV exposure, but prevention of cSCC from those changes has not been confirmed.

document_sections.heading: 11.2. Secondary prevention in immunocompromised patients
document_sections.content: Secondary strategies discussed for immunocompromised people include systemic chemoprevention and changes to immunosuppression. Evidence is concentrated in OTRs, and selection and sequencing remain uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 11.2.1. Systemic chemoprevention
document_sections.content: Retinoids, nicotinamide and capecitabine have been investigated as systemic preventive treatments in OTRs, with differing levels of evidence, tolerability and regulatory approval.

document_sections.heading: 11.2.1.1. Retinoids
document_sections.content: Three OTR randomized trials found significant reductions in AK and/or cSCC with retinoids, with an estimated 54% overall reduction in cSCC. Dose-limiting adverse effects include cheilitis, xerosis, alopecia, headache, musculoskeletal symptoms and hyperlipidaemia; approximately 14% discontinue treatment. Liver-function and lipid monitoring are required. A rebound rise in cSCC commonly occurs 3–4 months after stopping. Data outside OTRs are scarce, and comparable preventive efficacy for isotretinoin in OTRs is uncertain. Neither FDA nor EMA has approved retinoids for cSCC chemoprevention. Consensus opinion favours starting acitretin at a low dose, such as 10 mg/day, and increasing as tolerated to effective maintenance, for example up to 30 mg/ day. Optimal indications and dosing need further research. Potential rebound means treatment should be discussed as a long-term approach requiring laboratory monitoring.

document_sections.heading: 11.2.1.2. Nicotinamide
document_sections.content: Compared with systemic retinoids, trials found few adverse effects with nicotinamide and no need for laboratory monitoring. Prospective randomized evidence has not confirmed prevention of keratinocyte cancers in immunocompromised patients. Two small OTR trials suggested possible efficacy but lacked statistical power. A phase 3 trial compared nicotinamide 500 mg or placebo twice daily for 12 months in 158 OTRs with at least two keratinocyte cancers during the past 5 years. New cSCC counts did not differ significantly, and adverse-event profiles were similar. Poor recruitment left the trial underpowered. The investigators also suggested that transplant immunosuppressants’ effects on antitumour immunity and DNA repair might limit nicotinamide benefit.

document_sections.heading: 11.2.1.3. Capecitabine
document_sections.content: Capecitabine is an oral 5-fluorouracil prodrug. Limited observational evidence suggests cSCC prevention in OTRs, but dose-limiting fatigue, hand-foot syndrome, diarrhoea, nausea or vomiting, mucositis, anaemia and hyperuricemia or gout led to discontinuation in 43% of patients. It has no FDA/EMA approval for this indication, and optimal dosing is unknown. Trials are needed to determine patient selection, dosing, safety and longer-term efficacy.

document_sections.heading: 11.2.2. Modification of immunosuppression
document_sections.content: Changing immunosuppression could help prevent another cSCC, but evidence does not adequately define timing or method. Allograft type, individual tumour risk and the rate of new tumours should inform decisions.

document_sections.heading: Minimisation of immunosuppression and conversion to alternative immunosuppressive drugs
document_sections.content: Overall immunosuppression intensity may matter as much as any individual drug, but no robust measure guides intensity-based decisions. Evidence on which agents to reduce or stop is limited. Azathioprine carries particularly high cSCC risk compared with mycophenolate mofetil; evidence for important differences among calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) is weaker. Switching from a calcineurin inhibitor to belatacept may lower cSCC risk.

document_sections.heading: Conversion to mTOR inhibitors
document_sections.content: Several randomized trials found that switching from CNIs to mTOR inhibitors after a first cSCC reduces subsequent cSCC; switching after more than one cSCC produced a non-significant reduction. mTOR inhibitors do not appear to prevent a first post-transplant cSCC. A meta-analysis involving 5876 OTR from 21 RCTs found 56% fewer keratinocyte cancers with mTORi but also increased overall mortality, potentially reflecting higher doses in earlier trials. Delayed wound healing, diarrhoea, mucositis and peripheral oedema contribute to frequent discontinuation.

document_sections.heading: 11.3. Sequencing of cSCC prevention approaches
document_sections.content: Evidence is insufficient to establish optimal selection, starting thresholds and sequence of preventive treatments. In an OTR e-Delphi study, participants agreed on photoprotection and AK treatment but not on prevention after the first invasive cSCC. Despite randomized evidence, concern about adverse effects prevented consensus on mTORi conversion. For multiple cSCC accumulating slowly, modification of immunosuppression together with systemic chemoprevention was recommended, without agreement on the agent; inadequate OTR evidence was cited against routine nicotinamide. At accrual > 10/year, acitretin was recommended and was also the first choice for high-risk cSCC. Prospective trials are still needed to establish the best sequence.

document_sections.heading: 11.4. Surveillance
document_sections.content: Many post-transplant guidelines advise skin-cancer surveillance for all OTRs at least annually, but evidence that this prevents cSCC is limited, and risk-stratified approaches have been proposed. Education about photoprotection and AK treatment may be most useful before transplantation, although the cost-effectiveness of pre-transplant screening is unvalidated. After transplantation, baseline risk assessment and education on photoprotection, self-examination and early recognition are recommended according to age, gender, skin phototype and organ type. Later visit intervals depend on the initial risk assessment. Risk-prediction models can inform surveillance. Most supporting evidence concerns OTRs, although surveillance could also benefit other immunocompromised groups, particularly people with CLL or inflammatory bowel disease.

document_sections.heading: Box 9 Prevention of cSCC in solid organ transplant recipients.
document_sections.content: Evidence-based GPP. Education on regular skin surveillance, sun protection and sunscreen should be recommended; sunscreen evidence is Level of evidence: 4. Oral retinoids should be considered for OTRs with one or more cSCC (Level of evidence: 3). For the same population, conversion to mTOR inhibitors and modification of immunosuppression can each be discussed with transplant physicians (Level of evidence: 3 for each).

document_sections.heading: Summarizing box of recommendations
document_sections.content: The practice-point table consolidates, without changing them, the recommendations in Boxes 1–9: classify common primary and advanced disease; document and confirm suspected cSCC; recognize specified high-risk factors; tailor staging imaging to risk and findings; do not use SLNB as standard care; recommend UV-protection education; consider nicotinamide for eligible immunocompetent patients; and address surveillance, retinoids and possible immunosuppression changes with transplant recipients. It displays their respective grades A, GPP, GPP, B, GPP, X, GPP, C and GPP.
